unit.unitOverview: Tell the story of your own life: where you grew up, what shaped you, and what changed. Say what you used to do and no longer do, and describe a whole stretch of your past rather than single events. Say what was done for you, and add a comment on what you have just said without starting a new sentence.
unit.learningPath:
The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 6 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: a personal account, a short article and a form.
Questions: 10 about the three texts.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.
functions: Tell the story of your own life in order
Say what you used to do and no longer do

Say what was done for you, and who did it when that matters

visual.lectureScript:
Welcome to Level 3.
This level starts where Level 2 ended, and it opens with the hardest easy question there is: tell me about yourself.
People ask it in interviews, at a desk, on a first day, and at the end of a long evening.
It sounds simple, and it is not, because a life is not a list of events.
It is a few turning points with a lot of ordinary time in between.
This unit gives you the English for both: the turning points, and the stretches.

One thing to say before anything else.
Five of the six patterns in this unit sit on ground you have already covered.
That is deliberate, and it is not revision.
At this level the same pattern comes back wider, and each card tells you exactly what is new in it.
If a card looks familiar for the first two lines, keep reading. The third line is the one you came for.

Start with the words.
Six adjectives here bring their own preposition, and in Level 2 you learned that the preposition never changes.
Responsible for. Capable of. Keen on.
That is true of most of them, and for a few it is not, and those few are the first pattern card.
Keen on languages, but keen to start.
Proud of my daughter, but proud to say it.
Aware of the deadline, but aware that it had passed.
Disappointed with a thing, but disappointed in a person.
So the question is no longer which preposition belongs to this adjective.
It is what comes next: a noun, a verb, a clause, a person.

Then the stages of a life: childhood, upbringing, generation, background, milestone, turning point.
Two of those are close and not the same.
Your childhood is what happened to you. Your upbringing is what was done for you and taught to you.
A milestone marks a stage. A turning point changes the direction.

Now the patterns, and there are six.
The second one is used to, and this is the one card here that is new outright.
used to says a thing lasted for a stretch of the past and is not true now.
I used to work nights. Two words, and the contrast with today is already inside them.
Watch the question and the negative, because the d disappears after did.
Did you use to work here? I did not use to like it.

The third is the passive, and here is its increment.
In Level 2 you put a thing at the front. The roof was repaired. The cotton is grown.
A life story puts a person there instead. I was raised. We were told nothing.
And that opens something the thing-sentences never needed.
Some verbs have two objects. The company offered her the contract.
So you get a choice: she was offered the contract, or the contract was offered to her.
English picks the person nearly every time.
One thing to watch. At the front, her becomes she, him becomes he, me becomes I.

The fourth is the past continuous, and it is also an increment.
In Level 2 you used it for a background that something cut across: I was waiting when the call came.
It does a second job here. It holds a long stretch open.
That year I was working nights. Things were changing faster than we noticed.
The past simple would turn each of those into one finished event, and that is not what you mean.
One warning: a state verb stays simple. I knew her for years, never I was knowing her.

The fifth is a set of two-word verbs a life story cannot do without.
You already know how they work, so this card is about the set itself.
Grow up, bring up, move away, settle down, take after, look back on.
You grow up. Somebody else brings you up. Those two are not interchangeable.

The sixth is relative clauses, and you have most of it already.
Level 2 gave you who, whose and whom, and the commas around a detail that is extra.
Stage seven adds two things.
The first is why, for a reason. That is the reason why I stayed.
The second is bigger, and it is worth slowing down for.
There is a which that does not point at a noun at all. It points back at everything you just said.
I trained as an electrician, which was what my grandmother had wanted.
That which does not mean electrician. It means the whole of the first half.
And it always takes a comma, because it can never identify anything.
Drop the comma and it reads as pointing at the last noun, which changes the sentence.

The reading is a personal account of the year a factory closed.
Then an article about why we remember turning points at all.
And a contributor form for a community history project.
Read the form properly. Real forms ask what changed for you personally, and you will answer that one in writing later in this unit.

One last thing before you begin.
Everything you say about yourself in this unit can be invented.
Nobody is checking, nothing is submitted anywhere, and a made-up life uses exactly the same grammar as a real one.
If your own story is something you would rather not write down, invent one and practise on that.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

readings.title: The Year the Factory Closed
readings.setting: A small town, told forty years later
readings.passageScript:
I grew up in a town of four thousand people.
For most of my childhood the factory at the end of the road employed nearly all of them.
My grandmother brought me up. She had left school at twelve and she was not sentimental about work.
The factory was closed in my first year at secondary school. Nobody told us why.
That year my grandmother was working two jobs, and I hardly saw her before eight at night.
Gradually the shops on the main street closed as well.
Half my generation moved away, which changed the place completely.
I stayed, mostly because I was not aware of what else there was.
Eventually I trained as an electrician, which was what my grandmother had wanted for me all along.
I am not ashamed of any of it, and I am proud of the ones who left too.
Looking back on it now, the turning point was not the closure.
It was the evening my grandmother sat down and told me she was tired.
I had never heard her admit that before.

readings.title: Why We Remember Turning Points
readings.passageScript:
Ask anybody to tell the story of their life and they will give you four or five moments, not four or five thousand.
Memory is not a recording. It keeps what changed something and lets the rest go.
Researchers call these moments turning points, and most people place them between the ages of fifteen and thirty.
That is not because nothing happens later. It is because that is when most first things happen: the first job, the first move away, the first real choice.
A turning point is rarely obvious while it is going on.
It is built afterwards, when you look back and see where the road bent.
This is the reason why two people who lived through the same year will describe it differently.
One was working, the other was studying. One stayed, the other moved away.
The events were the same. The story is not, because a story is made of the parts you kept.

grammar.title: When the same adjective takes two prepositions
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 taught you that an adjective brings one small word with it, and that the small word never changes.
Responsible for. Capable of. Keen on.
That is true of most of them. For a few it is not, and those are the ones worth a card.
The adjective takes one preposition before a noun and a different one before a verb.
Or a different one for a person than for a thing.
The choice is not free. It changes what you are saying.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
keen ON a noun         I am keen on languages.
keen TO + verb         I am keen to start.

proud OF a noun        I am proud of my daughter.
proud TO + verb        I am proud to say it.

aware OF a noun        I was aware of the deadline.
aware THAT + clause    I was aware that it had passed.

disappointed WITH a thing   I was disappointed with the flat.
disappointed IN a person    I was disappointed in him.

Two that do NOT alternate, so you can stop worrying about them:
capable is always of. ashamed is almost always of.
After of the verb still takes -ing, as you already know: capable of running.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Choose: I am keen ___ languages, and keen ___ start in the spring.
1. Look at what comes after the first gap. languages is a noun.
2. A noun after keen takes on.
3. Look after the second gap. start is a verb.
4. A verb after keen takes to.
5. Same adjective, two prepositions, and neither is a mistake.
Answer: I am keen on languages, and keen to start in the spring.
grammar.commonMistake:
disappointed with and disappointed in are not interchangeable.
I was disappointed with him says what he produced let you down.
I was disappointed in him says HE let you down.
Use in only for a person, and only when you mean the person.
grammar.memoryTip: Ask what comes NEXT: a noun, a verb, a clause, a person. That chooses the preposition, not the meaning of the adjective.
grammar.practice:
Write the missing word. Four adjectives appear twice, with a different word each time.
1. I am keen ___ languages.
2. I am keen ___ start in the spring.
3. She was proud ___ her daughter.
4. She was proud ___ say she had trained them all.
5. I was not aware ___ the deadline.
6. I was not aware ___ it had already passed.
7. We were disappointed ___ the flat.
8. We were disappointed ___ him after the meeting.
grammar.answerKey:
1. on  2. to  3. of  4. to  5. of  6. that  7. with  8. in
Number 6 is the odd one out: aware that introduces a whole clause, not a noun.
Wrong on 7 and 8? with for a thing, in for a person.
6 or more right: good. Fewer: go by what comes NEXT, not by what the adjective means.

grammar.title: used to: the habit that stopped
grammar.explanation:
used to says a thing was true for a stretch of the past and is not true now.
It carries the contrast by itself, so you do not need to add any more.
I used to work nights. (I do not now.)
This one is new. Nothing below this level teaches it.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
I used to work nights.
She used to live near the sea.
We used to walk to school.

The question and the negative drop the d:
Did you use to work nights?
I did not use to like it.

used to works for a STATE as well as a habit:
I used to be afraid of the dark.

It has no present. For now, use the present simple:
Nowadays I work days.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Turn this into a used to sentence: I worked nights for six years. I do not now.
1. Ask whether the stretch is over. It is.
2. Ask whether the contrast with now is the point. It is.
3. Both yes, so used to fits.
4. used to takes a plain verb: used to work.
Answer: I used to work nights.
The six years can go or stay. used to already tells the listener it lasted.
grammar.commonMistake:
The d disappears after did, and it is easy to leave it in.
No: Did you used to work here?
Yes: Did you use to work here?
Same in the negative: I did not use to.
grammar.memoryTip: used to = it lasted, and it stopped. Both halves, in two words.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each one with used to.
1. I worked in a kitchen for three years. I do not now.
2. She lived with her grandmother. She does not now.
3. We walked everywhere. We drive now.
4. He was afraid of dogs as a child. He is not now.
Now write the question and the negative.
5. Ask somebody whether they lived here before.
6. Say that you did not like coffee before.
grammar.answerKey:
1. I used to work in a kitchen.  2. She used to live with her grandmother.
3. We used to walk everywhere.  4. He used to be afraid of dogs.
5. Did you use to live here?  6. I did not use to like coffee.
Wrong on 5 or 6? After did it is use to, with no d.
All six: good. Four or fewer: read the rule again and redo 5 and 6.

grammar.title: I was raised, she was offered: a person at the front
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 built the passive out of two pieces and put a THING at the front: the roof was repaired, the cotton is grown.
A life story puts a PERSON there instead, and that opens a form the thing-sentences never needed.
When a verb has two objects — somebody gives SOMEBODY SOMETHING — you choose which of the two goes to the front.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The part you already have: was or were + the past form.
The roof was repaired.            (a thing at the front)
I was raised by my grandmother.   (a person at the front)
We were told nothing for a week.

Verbs with TWO objects let you choose:
The company offered her the contract.
-> She was offered the contract.      (the person at the front)
-> The contract was offered to her.   (the thing at the front, and to appears)

English almost always chooses the person.
Others that work this way: give, tell, send, teach, pay, show.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Make this passive with the person at the front: The company offered her the contract.
1. Find the two objects: her, and the contract.
2. The person goes first, so start with her — but at the front it becomes she.
3. One person, and this is the past, so choose was.
4. offer becomes offered.
5. The other object stays exactly where it is.
Answer: She was offered the contract.
The company is dropped, because here it adds nothing.
grammar.commonMistake:
A person moving to the front changes her to she, him to he, me to I.
No: Her was offered the contract.
Yes: She was offered the contract.
At the front it is the subject, so it takes the subject form.
grammar.memoryTip: Two objects, two possible passives. English picks the person nearly every time.
grammar.practice:
Make each one passive, with the PERSON at the front.
1. My grandmother raised me.
2. Somebody told us nothing for a week.
3. The company offered her the contract.
4. The college gave him a place.
5. The supervisor showed her the whole building.
6. They paid her on the last day.
Now one with a thing at the front, for contrast.
7. Somebody boarded the windows up within a month.
grammar.answerKey:
1. I was raised by my grandmother. (keep by: she is the point of the sentence)
2. We were told nothing for a week.
3. She was offered the contract.
4. He was given a place at the college.
5. She was shown the whole building.
6. She was paid on the last day.
7. The windows were boarded up within a month.
Numbers 1 to 6 put a person at the front. Number 7 is the Level 2 shape, with a thing.
Watch me, us, him and her becoming I, we, he and she.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
grammar.title: That year I was working nights: the past over a long stretch
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 used the past continuous for a background that something cut across: I was waiting when the call came.
It does a second job as well, and that is what this card is for.
It holds a long stretch open — a year, a decade, a whole period of your life.
That year I was working nights and studying at weekends.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
was or were + -ing

The interruption you already know:
I was waiting when the call came.

The long stretch, which is new here:
That year I was working nights.
Things were changing faster than we noticed.
She was bringing up two children on her own.

Two stretches at once, joined by while or meanwhile:
He was studying at night while he worked all day.

The past simple would make each one a single finished event.
The continuous keeps it open across the whole stretch.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Choose the form: That year I ___ (work) nights and I hardly saw anybody.
1. Ask whether this is one event or a period. That year is a period.
2. A period you lived inside takes the past continuous.
3. I takes was.
4. work becomes working.
Answer: That year I was working nights and I hardly saw anybody.
worked would have made a whole year sound like one finished act.
grammar.commonMistake:
A state verb does not take the continuous, however long the stretch.
No: I was knowing her for years.
Yes: I knew her for years.
know, own, believe and understand stay simple.
grammar.memoryTip: One event, past simple. A stretch you lived inside, past continuous.
grammar.practice:
Choose the past simple or the past continuous.
1. That year I ___ (work) nights.
2. The power ___ (go) off while I was cooking.
3. Things ___ (change) gradually through the whole decade.
4. She ___ (bring) up two children on her own at the time.
5. I ___ (know) him for years before I asked.
6. Meanwhile, the rest of us ___ (wait) outside.
7. He ___ (apply) for the course in the spring.
8. Through those months I ___ (sleep) in the afternoons.
grammar.answerKey:
1. was working  2. went  3. were changing  4. was bringing  5. knew
6. were waiting  7. applied  8. was sleeping
Wrong on 5? know is a state verb and stays simple however long the stretch.
Wrong on 2 or 7? Each is one event, not a period.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Grew up, brought up, settled down: the set a life story runs on
grammar.explanation:
You already know how these work: two words, one meaning, and the object sometimes sits in the middle.
What you need here is the particular set.
Six of them carry almost every life story, and three are easy to confuse, because all three are about where you lived.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
grow up      = become an adult somewhere.    I grew up near the sea.
bring up     = raise a child.               She brought up three children.
move away    = leave the place you lived.   We moved away in 1974.
settle down  = stop moving and stay.        They settled down at last.
take after   = resemble an older relative.  I take after my father.
look back on = think about the past now.    I look back on it fondly.

The three that get confused:
YOU grow up. Somebody else BRINGS you up. A place, you MOVE AWAY from.

Splitting works the way it already did:
She brought up three children.  ->  She brought them up.
I look back on it.  NOT  I look it back on.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Fill the gap: My grandmother ___ ___ three children on her own.
1. The meaning is raised them, not became an adult.
2. Raise a child is bring up.
3. The story is in the past, so bring becomes brought.
4. There is an object, three children, and it can follow the pair.
Answer: My grandmother brought up three children on her own.
With a pronoun it has to split: she brought them up.
grammar.commonMistake:
grow up is about the person growing. bring up is about whoever raised them.
No: My grandmother grew me up.
Yes: My grandmother brought me up.
Or: I grew up with my grandmother.
grammar.memoryTip: If a noun can sit in the middle, a pronoun must. If it cannot, neither can.
grammar.practice:
Complete each one with a verb from the card, in the right tense.
1. I ___ ___ in a town of four thousand people.
2. My grandmother ___ ___ three children on her own.
3. We ___ ___ when I was eleven and never went back.
4. After years of moving, they finally ___ ___ .
5. Everyone says I ___ ___ my father.
6. I ___ ___ on that year with no regret at all.
Now rewrite each of these with a pronoun.
7. She brought up three children.
8. I look back on that year.
grammar.answerKey:
1. grew up  2. brought up  3. moved away  4. settled down  5. take after  6. look back
Number 6 is look back ON, so the full verb is three words.
7. She brought them up.  8. I look back on it. (this one never splits)
Wrong on 1 or 2? You grow up. Somebody else brings you up.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: The reason why, and the which that points back
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 gave you who, whose and whom, and the two commas around a detail that is extra.
Stage 7 adds two things neither of those covers.
One is why, which joins a clause to a reason.
The other is a which that does not point at a noun at all. It points back at everything you just said.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
why, after a reason:
That is the reason why I stayed.
I never asked why she had left.
You may drop either half: the reason I stayed, or why I stayed.

which, pointing back at a WHOLE clause, always after a comma:
I trained as an electrician, which was what she had wanted.
He never once complained, which surprised everybody.
Half the town moved away, which changed the place completely.

To tell them apart, ask what which refers to:
The factory, which employed most of the town, closed.  -> the factory (a noun)
The factory closed, which emptied the main street.     -> the whole event

A clause-which ALWAYS takes a comma, because it can never identify anything.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Join these: I trained as an electrician. That was what my grandmother had wanted.
1. Ask what the second sentence is about. Not electrician — the whole of the first sentence.
2. Pointing back at a whole clause takes which.
3. A clause-which always takes a comma in front of it.
4. Drop That was and start with which.
Answer: I trained as an electrician, which was what my grandmother had wanted.
grammar.commonMistake:
Without the comma, which reads as pointing at the last noun.
I trained as an electrician which was what she wanted.
That says the JOB was what she wanted, not the training.
The comma is what makes it point back at everything.
grammar.memoryTip: which after a comma means everything I just said. which with no comma means the noun in front of it.
grammar.practice:
Join each pair with why or which.
1. That is the reason. I stayed.
2. I trained as an electrician. That was what my grandmother had wanted.
3. He never complained. That surprised everybody.
4. Half the town moved away. That changed the place completely.
5. I never asked. Why had she left?
6. The factory employed most of the town. It closed in 1974. (point at the factory)
grammar.answerKey:
1. That is the reason why I stayed.
2. I trained as an electrician, which was what my grandmother had wanted.
3. He never complained, which surprised everybody.
4. Half the town moved away, which changed the place completely.
5. I never asked why she had left.
6. The factory, which employed most of the town, closed in 1974.
Number 6 is the Level 2 shape: which pointing at a noun, between two commas.
Numbers 2 to 4 are the new one: which pointing back at the whole sentence.
5 or more right: good.
